extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, historians of law/policy, and policymakers interested in poor laws, labour mobility, wage regulation, and the theory of rent
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a classical political economy treatise (Adam Smith) describing the English poor-laws and settlement statutes, wage- and price-regulation practices, and a foundational theory of rent (how rent is determined by fertility, situation, and market prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish responsibility for the poor (43rd Elizabeth c.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 43d of Elizabeth, c. 2. every parish should be bound to provide for its own poor, and overseers of the poor should be annually appointed, who, with the church-wardens, should raise, by a parish rate, competent sums for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute imposes the necessity of local provision; it makes the question 'who are the poor of each parish' legally important and grounds subsequent settlement rules and removal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement by forty days undisturbed residence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 13th and 14th of Charles II enacted that forty days undisturbed residence should gain any person a settlement in any parish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within forty days two justices could remove a new inhabitant upon complaint unless he rented a tenement of ten pounds a-year or could give security judged sufficient by the justices. This was the old common route to acquiring settlement, but it became practicably difficult by later statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to forty days rule: tenement of £10/year or sufficient security
rubrics_metrics.description: A newcomer could avoid removal within the forty-day period if he either rented a tenement of ten pounds a-year, or could give such security for the discharge of the parish as the justices should judge sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The security required was left to the discretion of the justices and often more than what labourers could provide; purchase of a freehold under £30 was insufficient to gain settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-in-writing requirement (1st James II)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 1st of James II it was enacted that the forty days undisturbed residence necessary to gain a settlement should be accounted only from the time of his delivering notice, in writing, of the place of his abode and the number of his family, to one of the church-wardens or overseers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aimed to curb fraud (hidden arrivals gaining a settlement by simply hiding forty days) by starting the clock only after written notice to parish officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-in-church requirement (3rd William III)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 3rd of William III the forty days residence should be accounted only from the publication of such notice in writing on Sunday in the church, immediately after divine service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication made the notice public, further enabling parishioners to object and reducing clandestine settlements; Burn notes that even then actual gaining of settlement by this route was rare and the statute served more to force parishes to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four alternative routes to settlement without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute appointed four other ways by which a settlement might be gained without any notice delivered or published: (1) by being taxed to parish rates and paying them; (2) by being elected into an annual parish office and serving in it a year; (3) by serving an apprenticeship in the parish; (4) by being hired into service there for a year, and continuing in the same service during the whole of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes practical limits: parishes rarely tax new-comers or elect them to offices; apprentices are rarely married; the law also expressly disallows married servants from gaining settlement by being hired for a year, so these paths were of limited use to ordinary labourers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction: married servants and apprentices
rubrics_metrics.description: No married man can well gain any settlement by either of the two last ways; an apprentice is scarce ever married; and it is expressly enacted that no married servant shall gain any settlement by being hired for a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits the effectiveness of service/apprenticeship as means for family men to secure settlement; it also discouraged customary annual hiring practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice discretion and minimum security (freehold < £30 insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: What security the justices shall require is left altogether to their discretion; but they cannot well require less than thirty pounds, it having been enacted that the purchase of a freehold estate of less than thirty pounds value shall not gain any person a settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since labourers could not provide such security, discretionary demands made gaining settlement by security practically impossible for the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate system (8th and 9th William III)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 8th and 9th of William III it was enacted that if any person should bring a certificate from the parish where he was last legally settled, subscribed by the church-wardens and overseers and allowed by two justices of the peace, every other parish should be obliged to receive him; he should not be removable merely for being likely to become chargeable, but only upon his becoming actually chargeable; and the parish which granted the certificate should be obliged to pay maintenance and removal expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certificates made receiving parishes accept responsibility but also prevented the certificated person from gaining a settlement in the new parish by notice, service, apprenticeship, or paying rates — only renting a tenement of £10/year or serving a year in a parish office might give settlement. Servants/apprentices of a certificated man could not gain settlement either (12th Queen Anne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and normative guidance about certificates (Burn's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certificates prevent newcomers from gaining settlement locally, ensure responsibility is known, and oblige the granting parish to bear costs if they become chargeable; thus 'certificates ought always to be required by the parish where any poor man comes to reside, and they ought very seldom to be granted by that which he purposes to leave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctor Burn observes certificates protect parishes from burdens and are generally prudent for receiving parishes, though they can harshly bind individuals to a parish 'as it were for life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish officers' discretionary power to grant certificates (mandamus rejected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting or refusing a certificate is altogether discretionary in the parish officers; a mandamus to compel officers to sign a certificate was rejected by the Court of King's Bench as a 'very strange attempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal precedent confirms strong local discretion, limiting judicial compulsion to force certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of settlement laws on labour mobility and wage disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of settlements gives an obstruction to a poor man who would carry his industry from one parish to another without a certificate; it thus probably explains the very unequal price of labour in places at no great distance from one another in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith contrasts this with Scotland and other countries without settlement difficulties, where wages vary smoothly with distance from demand centres; settlement laws make parishes artificial barriers, preventing labour supply from equalizing wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative claim: removal without misdemeanor violates liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove a man who has committed no misdemeanour from the parish where he chooses to reside is 'an evident violation of natural liberty and justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that despite its injustice, this oppression was widely tolerated and not the object of general popular clamour like other abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical decline of statutory wage regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anciently it was usual to rate wages by general laws or by particular orders; both these practices have now gone entirely into disuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith (quoting Burn) argues that minute statutory regulation of wages is inappropriate: if equal wages were enforced, emulation and industry would be stifled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory wage cap (8th George III for London tailors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 8th of George III prohibits, under heavy penalties, all master tailors in London, and five miles round it, from giving, and their workmen from accepting, more than two shillings and sevenpence halfpenny a-day, except in the case of a general mourning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith criticizes such laws when they favor masters; he notes that counsel to the legislature often come from masters, producing biased regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law favoring payment in money, not in goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The law which obliges masters in several trades to pay their workmen in money, and not in goods, is 'quite just and equitable' as it prevents masters from pretending to pay in goods while not providing equivalent monetary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith treats this as an example of legislation that fairly protects workers without imposing real hardship on masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry in enforcement of combinations (masters vs workmen)
rubrics_metrics.description: When masters combine to reduce wages they commonly enter into private bonds or agreements enforceable by penalties; were workmen to combine similarly the law would punish them severely — the 8th of George III often enforces the regulation masters seek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith highlights a legal asymmetry: the law tolerates or supports master combinations but punishes worker combinations, leading to unfair outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assize of bread as legacy of price regulation; general preference for competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The assize of bread is the only remnant of ancient price-fixing; where there is no exclusive corporation competition will regulate price much better than any assize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes attempts to fix prices for provisions historically, and argues that in most contexts competition is superior, with assize being increasingly unnecessary and often ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rent as the highest tenant can afford to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent, considered as the price paid for the use of land, is naturally the highest which the tenant can afford to pay in the actual circumstances of the land; the landlord tries to leave the tenant no greater share than sufficient to keep up stock, pay labour, and ordinary profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'natural rent' is the portion of produce or price over and above what is necessary for the tenant's maintenance and ordinary profits; landlords aim to capture the surplus, making rent effectively a monopoly price determined by what the farmer can give.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent not primarily compensation for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent of land is frequently not merely a reasonable profit for the stock laid out by the landlord upon its improvement; the landlord demands rent even for unimproved land and charges for natural advantages (e.g., kelp shores or access to fisheries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement-related charges are additions to an original rent; improvements may be made by tenant stock and on renewal the landlord typically demands rent increases as if he had paid for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent determined by fertility and situation; transport costs matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent of land varies with its fertility and with its situation; land near a town gives greater rent than equally fertile land remote from market because carriage costs reduce the surplus available from distant land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements in roads, canals, and navigable rivers diminish carriage expense, equalize remote parts with market areas, encourage cultivation of remoter lands, and break local monopoly effects that raise rents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent as effect, wages/profit as causes of price
rubrics_metrics.description: High or low wages and profit are the causes of high or low price; high or low rent is the effect of it — rent enters into the composition of price differently from wages and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ordinary price exceeds what is necessary to replace stock and pay labour/profit, the surplus naturally goes to the rent of land; if not, the commodity can be brought to market but affords no rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of produce: always affords rent vs sometimes affords rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Some parts of the produce of land must always afford a rent (because demand always yields a price above what is necessary to bring them to market); others sometimes may or may not afford rent depending on circumstances; and relative values change during periods of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith uses examples (bread vs butcher's meat, pasture vs corn) to show how demand, relative production costs, and agricultural development change which produce yields rent and how land is used over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local demand and agricultural technique can alter relative rents
rubrics_metrics.description: Local circumstances (e.g., demand for milk or forage near a town) and agricultural practices (artificial grasses, turnips, carrots, cabbages) can raise the rent of pasture relative to corn or reduce the historical superiority of butcher's meat relative to bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These local and technical factors can make pasture more valuable than corn-land in particular situations; such advantages are often temporary as broader improvements (inclosure, artificial grasses) shift relative profitability.
